blocks.x: You can start off by getting your name.
Yeah. My name is Louis P. James Sr.
When were you born?
And you had the exact date?
Yeah, 9th of April.
9th of April, 1890. And what town were you born in?
Gibbettel, Louisiana.
Can you tell us a little bit about your father and your folks, if they played music?
Well, my father didn't play any music. He was a farmer. He used to fire and cook on a steamboat, you know.
Was that on a bayou out there?

Yeah, by the push. And I had five brothers of us. We all played music. Were you the oldest? No, no. I had two older than me and two younger than me. My youngest brother is still now in California. He played saxophone and kindly. He's a wonderful musician. Yeah. And I also played saxophone.
Can you tell us about the first instrument that you took up? What did you start on?
The first instrument that I took up was my heel. Just a bit of something you took? And then a head comb. A comb? Yeah, a comb. Paper? Yeah, with paper. See?
Did it stomp your heel too?
No, I rubbed my heel on the, you know, and made base. Oh, yeah? Oh, I see.
On a box or something?

No, on the floor. On the floor? Yeah, on the floor. Yeah, it was fine. And after that, my cousin and my brother used to play mandolin and guitar, you know? And by listening to them, I just liked myself, you know, just by listening. So I learned how to play mandolin and my first song that I played was Home Sweet Home and I was hitting a note every five minutes, you know, and my sister called me to go get a bucket of water from the well. So I said, we used to call it Chook, the nickname, you know? And I said, yeah, I said, yeah, there's a dime. I said, go ahead. I didn't want to stop, you see? I just continued trying to play Home Sweet Home. So that goes on for a good while, about a couple of months. So I began to play Home Sweet Home. And the band leader, Joe Gabriel, who was my band leader, but that was his instrument I was playing on, you know? He played mandolin and violin. So I didn't want him to catch me playing on his instrument because I didn't know whether he was like it or not.
Sure.

Sure. So when I did learn how to play Home Sweet Home, I said, I'm going to let him yell what I can do. Sure enough, when he came in, I said, Joe, get your get-that. He used to play get-that too. He used to play. So I played Home Sweet Home. He said, that's fine. I said, oh, I've got him some now. I was so glad that he didn't call at me about playing on his instrument. So after that, I learned Home Sweet Home on the violin. Then I picked up the violin. See? He said, that's fine. Did you have anybody to help you much at all? No lesson. Nobody. No lesson. See? No, I just couldn't get him going. No. I just couldn't get him going. You know? I went to play the same thing on the violin that I played on the violin. So I kept on until I got the swing of it, you know. Then I played Home Sweet Home on the violin. So he said, that's just fine.
Did you have anybody to help you much at all? Any lessons? No, no. No lesson.
Nobody. See? I just picked it up. In fact, sir, when the John Road show came to Thibodeau, George Backe was playing Clownet, you know. George who? Backe.
Backe.
Yeah.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

And of course I had been playing violin and violin, but I didn't play the piano. So I, he was playing, he was playing that song about, that song, you know. And it went all through me, you know. I just got a trill out of that, you know, the sound, you know, that harmony from that clarinet, you know. And it stayed with me. See? I said, the last thing I'm going to do, I said, I'm going to learn how to play clarinet.
When was that you heard, George Backe?
That was about 19, 19, 19, 19, somewhere around that time. I imagine it was long in that time. The Robichaux's band came up?
Yeah, Robichaux, yeah, yeah. He played like a clarinet solo on that, huh?
Well, no, he was playing the band, the whole band. The whole band. The whole band.
Remember who else was in the band then when you heard them?

Yeah, Backe and Robichaux and Contrat I think was playing drums. And he had William from Homer, Louisiana. Yeah, yeah, yeah. I think James Williams, I think his name was James Williams. How did Robichaux play on violin?
Was he really good? Was he left handed? Was that? He was left handed. Was he really a good? Oh yeah, oh yeah, it is.

At that time, you know, he was just recognized, you know. And the music, we was playing two, four time music at that time, you know. But now it's what you call, you know, it's even more two, four time music.
Was that mostly ragtime you mean or what?
Well, it's kind of Dixieland, you know, but just the same as common time, you know. Yeah.
You played a little slower beat? Yeah, yeah.
A little slower. Slow beat. Yeah.
I was wondering about that band you mentioned, Joe. Joe Gabriel, oh yeah. What kind of band was that?

Oh, we had a wonderful band. See, Claiborne William and Joe Gabriel, see, his four brothers played with Joe Gabriel, you see. He was our band leader. And I played saxophone and clarinet. At least I learned how to play clarinet. So they thought I was so apt, they wanted to improve the band, so they decided to get me a saxophone. Well, I learned how to play saxophone from the message, see. See, that's the way I liked. I didn't have nobody playing saxophone at that time.
And you started on your mandolin and violin. Did you ever have any books that you learned to read or just learned by head?

No, I learned how to read by, well, you might as well say, by just looking and listening, see. Yes. I used to have a discussion around from Tibeto to New Orleans, so I'd always go to John Robesher and buy his music, you know. Yes. Before I, when I get back home, I already know the air of the song, you understand. Yeah. And I just learn the notes, see. Figure out the notes for it. And I know it nicely, you see. I know it nicely, see. You sort of sing the notes to yourself?
Yeah, yeah. Uh huh.

On the way home. Well, it happened that I wouldn't go to bed when you get back home by twelve, one o'clock, you know, on the excursion. And by knowing that song, by air, I said, well, let me read it before I go to bed, see. Yeah. So I just kept on, and that's why I know so much about music that I should know, because I learned how to read first sight, you see. Yeah. And then we'd have our rehearsal, you know, and put it down. See, I was so apt by heart, you know, well, I didn't need no music.
Well, these four brothers, were they the Gabriel brothers? No, no. Or your brothers?

Yeah, my brothers. All four of you. Yeah, four of us. See, my four oldest brothers, a guitar player. Then my next brother next to me, he played trombone and clarinet and bass. And my youngest brother in California now, he played saxophone, violin, and clarinet. And his son playing music too. Skeet, they call him. He played with the pijon.
What pieces did you play? What kind of pieces? Were they popular songs or ragtime marches, waltzes?

Yeah, I played all, let me see, at that time he was playing a song that I played in my time. The first song I played on the clarinet was Next to Your Mother, Who Do Your Love. And I can't get the copy of that song. I never saw it either. Yeah. Da Next to your mother, Who Do Your Love. And well we used to play shardies and mazookas at that time, you know? And card drill. Oh yeah. Well when I first started playing music we had a set of two waltzes, I learned how to play two waltzes, two two steps, two shardies, two mazookas, and then you come with your five pieces card drill, see? But now I learned a set of that, you see? Just like you say you eat rice today and bean, and tomorrow you eat bean and rice. And the song lasts a long time in my time, you know? Yeah, yeah.
How long would you play it though?

Oh we played that over two years you might as well say. Yeah, yeah. It was new, you see? The way we twist it, you see? And we used to have recess, we used to have recess too, you know? When we play a ball, we would start at nine o'clock and play, we have two or three resets before twelve o'clock, see? About five or ten minutes. Yeah. And we'd go back and play the same thing over again, there's bean and rice. And when we have a next recess we'd play rice and bean, see? And the dance was over, see? Yeah. That's pretty good.
Well each tune you'd play quite a while then, wouldn't you?

Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. I mean you played a set, you see? Every time you played the two waltzes, when you get on the stand, you played two waltzes, and two two steps, and two shorties, and two mazurkas, then you played the five pieces for the card drill, you see? Well now you take a recess at the card drill, see? Then when you go back you start two waltzes again, see? You have to play your two waltzes first.
Yeah, but you mix them around and stuff.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, see? So after you have three recess, well it's not time for the dance to break up, then you play home feet home, see?
Did they have many other bands up there, dance orchestras?

Well no, there's a few bands there, Joe Gabriel, and uh, Claiborne William, you know? Yeah, he was in Donaldsonville. Donaldsonville, and they had a band in Crowley I think, the Bower Boys in Oregon City. I played with them too, Johnny Bower and Willie Bower and...
Did they have any brass bands?
Oh yeah, they had the yucca band, yucca band. My uncle, I had two uncles played in the brass band. Oh, they had a wonderful brass band. Right in Thibodeau? Yes sir.
What was it called, your name?
The name of the band was... The, the, the, the, uh, yucca band.
Eurica?
No, yucca.
Yurca? Yeah. Yurca? Oh, oh, oh, I'm trying to get a yucca band.

How many players did they have in that band? They had about, they had about fifteen or eighteen. Big band? Yeah, a big band. This boy played Jowles, played Jowles, you remember? Yeah. And he was, he was a drummer in that band. The drummer.
Yeah.
He played bass drum. Bass drum. And his brother played snare drum, Al Badger. He got his son down there playing a lot.
Yes, Al Badger. Al Badger.

Yeah, yeah. Well, his daddy played drum in Gabriel's band. Yes. Oh, we had, he was a good drummer too, you know, through Ed Dixieland. That's, that's the only musician that they had in the all at that time, the country boy, see, when he come here, and they didn't read, you know. Most of the musicians didn't read. That's why, first, when I started playing with him, well now, Basset was playing right across the street from where we was playing, you see. And so first we put that music up there, you know, and that would run him away. What if, and he couldn't read it. He couldn't read, see. So, I just, that's what makes me love Basset Day. He's a wonderful guy, you know, if you want to know it. So, him and Joe Gabriel, well, that's the only two that I can, you know, vouch to see that I make the grades, see. Because Gabriel is living yet, you know, but he don't play. He's pretty sick. Where is he?
Up in Thibodeau, yeah.
Up in Thibodeau, yeah. Oh, he was a wonderful violin player. And when we, see, we didn't play for colored people. Most of them white dancers.
Most of the white dancers.
And we got, where were they given?
Balls, balls. Where did they give those? They had some halls up there?

Oh yeah, Thibodeau, Homer, Louisiana, and, and, uh, Morgan City, Patterson, Louisiana, Franklin, and, uh, we was out every night. And the only way that, uh, they could get out there on holiday night, they would have to high on that night. For the next year. For the next year. For the next year. For the next year. For the next year. For the next year. For the next year.

That's the way we was booked. And never disappointed nobody one time. Every time you see the band you see the same faces. And you were respected. White people used to get up out there and give us their rum whenever we'd go out to play. Transportation, everything paid, you know. Didn't have to worry about no...eating, neither drink, and sleep.
How much did the dancers pay in those days?

We was getting six dollars a night. Six dollars a man. Six dollars a man. Wasn't bad, wasn't it? No. We already got a dollar and a half a night in the district. That was big money, see. I got two and a half a night on Saturday night when I first started playing. That's all I got. And could live a whole week. Well I was working in the field for two bits a day. Yeah. That's what made me learn how to play music so soon, see. Because I wanted my car in time. I wore that in the field. Mm-hmm.
Yes. Oh. So I...
And your father played any...you say he didn't play any...
No, he didn't.
Did he sing or anything?

No, he...but he loved it. He loved it. I never thought... No, yeah. My uncle, see, I ain't heard that from my uncles. See, I and my uncles, I... They were musicians? Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. A timbre horn player and one of the bass horn player.
Oh yeah.
Did they play in the brass band?
Oh yeah. With Giles and all... He used to play a violin, cymbal, voice. Your uncle?
Yeah. Your uncle? Yeah. And...

None of them are still living, I guess? No, no. They're both dead. And my oldest brother died too, you know, and they're the bass player. Two brothers dead and three of us living. Of course, the one that don't play no more, he used to play guitar. And when we play home, see, at home, that they come in offers twenty dollars a man. He said, no, he's tired, he's going home, he put his guitar down. That's just how he was. But Lord, you don't play home, see, home, you play there all night, you know, all day. But don't play home, see, home. He won't quit. He don't lay there, right? Well, he just feel like he'll knock off when he plays there.
Ah, I see. Yeah. When did you first come to New Orleans? I came...
I came... Well, I came in 1915 and I went back.
How long were you here then?
Well, I just told the district closed down, you know.
I mean, when you first came here that time.
Well, I came here, I went back after the district closed down. Oh, I see.
You must have been here quite a while, weren't you?
I said, no, it was 1915, I think. Oh. I came, yeah. And you went back? I went for Wooden Central Bank, you know. And that's why I'd been knowing Manny, you know. Yes.
Where did you work when you moved down in the district then? Where did you play there? At the Villa.
At the Villa.
At the Villa. Yeah. You did your first job when you moved to the city. No, I played around the city.

I played with Frankie Duesen and Jack Carey, you know. I played, you know, in the... What did you play then? Your... The spring clarinet. Your clarinet. Yeah, the spring clarinet. Then I made records with Louis Domaine, you know, with the tenor sax. Oh, yes.

Can you tell us about when you first took up the clarinet? You say you heard George Bocquet and he inspired you to take it up. Yeah, that's right. That's right. Where did you get the clarinet and when and all?

Well, I... I happened to buy a... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... A... And... Uh... I... 된... 된... 된... ! They bought me alto sax when I was playing clarinet. I pawned that and I never could get it out any time before I got it out. I pawned it one carnival. I didn't play, you know. I didn't worry about it. I couldn't get it out. So he just bought my ticket. Just like now, I'm playing clarinet, but you know, after I couldn't get going with a good trumpet player, well I just, you know, I mean this rock and roll stuff come out, well I don't fall for that kind of stuff and just make me forget about it, you know.
Do you have any lessons on clarinet? Anybody help you?
The boy Presley Goff, he used to be down on Tulu Street, he's in Tibbetul. He played music too, you know. Presley Goff.
And he helped you some with the clarinet?
He learned me to scale. He learned how to play clarinet himself.
How long did it take you to play the clarinet?
Oh it didn't take me long. That's what I'm saying now, it didn't take me long. After I learned to scale.
You went out on the job then pretty soon.

Well that was my first piece on the job, next to your mother, who do you love. At that time we was playing, oh I just can't recall the names of the pieces. But anyhow, we used to cut the name off our music, you know, whenever we'd get it. Oh yeah, I've heard of it. When the songs came out about, I'd like to be with you one hour of the night, I'd like to marry you. Well, the white girls, you know, the iron girl. Well, that's why we were so respected because we stayed in our place, you know. Color didn't mean that, see, I'm a Catholic, see. And Catholic, uh, permit you to be as one, you understand, see. And I never destroyed my Catholic girls, I always destroyed the Protestant girls because I felt like doing the right thing towards my color, you see. It's just like I respected the white people, see, I stayed in my place, you see. So, finished talking about those songs. Oh yeah. We told them, they used to bring bulkheads and put it out to our leader's speech, you know, well, quite natural. That didn't look so good down there, South, you see. So we told them, our band leader said, well now Joe, whenever that you, uh, you know, they come in there for the number, said let them see for themselves. See, keep the name on the music, see. That'll cut out, uh, suspicion, you see. So, uh, that's why we started keeping the name on the piece of that piece, you see. We used to get our music from, uh, from Serious and Robots.
Serious and Robots.
Yeah, yeah, yeah. You see, that's why I said his music comes two, four times, you know.
Was the music, uh, the dance music much different down here in the city than up there in Tippin-Dawg? Did it sound, did they play different down here, different beat? Oh no, no, no.

Well, uh, the different that it was, the boys down here learned by air, you see. And by replaying our music was quite natural, you know, that, that made the difference. Yeah. See, but, uh, see a fella can get more out of a song by playing in their own way than you can playing the other fellas for music, you see. Of course it makes you be more together when everybody in the band is reading, you know. Well, everybody got their part. Well, that band sounds good. But you take a fella got a, uh, a band that nobody reading, well they're all making just whatever they want. But if they can get together in doing that, they can get a lot of music out of it, you know.
When you, when you came down here, what was the first band you played with? You mentioned Jack Carey and, uh, Dooson, but was the first?
Well, uh, first band I called myself playing with was, uh, uh, Amos Riley. Oh, Amos Riley. Yeah.
Who else was in the band? Joe Howard. Joe Howard, yeah.

Yeah. Yeah, yeah. Well, I played with him with, uh, with the, with the first, you see, but he wasn't recommending it, uh, first to me, you see. What'd you, uh, be about, uh, uh, 15, did you say you moved here? Yeah, that, that, that was about, uh, uh, that was about the 15th, 1915. See?
During the First World War then? Yeah, yeah. The war had started. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
And, uh, if I'm not mistaken, I, I think I came on that in, in 1913. In 13. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah.

Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. 1913. Before the war. Yeah, before the war. Yeah, before the war. Because I, uh, Chris Gabriel, you see. Mm-hmm. And, uh, at least my wife came down, yeah. And I called myself coming down, yeah, not to wait. Yeah. I was in business up there. Well, the thing had got panty clothes on, you know?
Well, what kind of business did you have up there?

I had a pool room and a soft drink stand and beer and, uh, a boxing ring. Oh, all of that. Yeah, all of that, you see. Of course, we'd play music most every night, you see. Well, I just, every day was Sunday with us and a dollar at that time was a dollar. You know, you could, you could, you could so much out of a dollar, see. Yeah. On your own home and everything. Mm-hmm. People, you didn't have to spend your money. People made their own garden and raised their chicken and, like, yeah. People were living out there, you know. People on the plantation, well, they had no rent to pay. Yeah.
You see.

Of course, after they stopped moving in town off the plantation, you know, paying rent, and then working on the plantation, well, that kind of, it's just like today. That's all there. The thing is so high now, a dollar no, no value nothing. Yeah. No value nothing. See.
Can you tell us some more about Amos Riley's band, where they played?
Well, uh, Amos Riley, he used to play for different parties, you know. And, uh, nobody played, you know, big dance hall or nothing. Yeah.
Mostly private parties. Yeah, yeah, parties, see.

He used to get those lawn parties at the time. Okay. And, uh, played with Rene a couple of times, that long part. Kid Rene? Yeah, Kid Rene. And, uh, his brother was playing drums. Then I played with, uh, Pajot. Willie Pajot.
Yeah. Parnett.
And I played with, uh, I played with Robichot at, uh, at, uh, Palace, uh, couple of times.
The theater. Yeah, yeah. Uh, what instrument did you play all those bands with, uh, those? Still playing it? I played with, uh, still playing it.
Still playing it? I played with, uh, with Amos Riley. But, you know, when I started playing with Lewisty Man, I had my B Tenor. The B Tenor. Yeah. When did you take up the bass?
The string bass?

Well, I, used to play bass, but I had taken it up after my brother died. See? Mm-hmm. See? In fact, I had bought a bass, so I let him have it, you see? Mm-hmm. And I just let him use it, but after he died. When did he die?
About then? Just late years?
Yeah.
My brother's been dead now, but he died in about 30, 35, I think. Yes. Yeah.
Can you tell us some more about Frankie Dewson's band, or, or, who you played with then?

Well, Frankie Dewson, uh, uh, I never did play with his, his band, but I played, he played on, on Lewisty Man's band, see? Well, he was with Lewisty Man. Yeah, he was with Lewisty Man. Me and Lewisty Man and, uh, and Wilkin LaBeth. You remember Wilkin LaBeth? Yes.
I don't know. I heard of him.
And, uh, and L. Gabriel, Manny Gabriel, Clarence Gabriel at least, was playing the band.
That would be after you left Jack Carey's band, would it?
Oh yeah, yeah, yeah.
Quite a while.

Well I've never called myself on the band as a member, you know, but I've played with him. I've never called myself a member of, uh, no band but Lewisty Man. Mm-hmm. See, I only, yeah, that's the only band that I consider myself playing in a band, you know?
But you probably have played with a lot of other bands.

Oh yeah, like, uh, played with, uh, Jack Carey and, uh, Frankie Dewson, and played with, uh, Willie Alpey, not Willie, Earl. Earl, the job one way. No, no, the trumpet player was, Percy. Percy. Percy, yeah, yeah, Percy.
Yeah, yeah, Percy.
Well I played with his band, and I played with, uh, the other band I played with, what should I, uh, with, uh, Earl, uh, Foster. You know Earl Foster?
I don't know him, but I don't know him.

Uh, uh, uh, well he had, well my brother used to play with him. That's, that's why I said, I'm sorry you haven't never heard him play saxophone. Oh, he's a wonderful saxophone player. That's why I'm asking to get to California, see? Because his son plays, plays saxophone too, you know, he used to play with, uh, Pijon. So it is up there now. Of course my brother's in the pool room business.
Oh, out there in California. In California.

And he don't care much about it because he was playing around it with Earl almost every night for me. But somehow he left. Just, didn't want to stay anymore. Just like I feel. I don't, I'm getting tired of it.
A lot of people like California very much.
Well you see, you get too old in a place and people don't, uh, give you the proper respect. stuff
I know what you mean. But if I get away from you, I believe I can make it.
I was going to ask who else was in Jack Carey's band when you played with him or when you heard him even when he was in the band.
Jack Carey's band, but this boy, oh, what's that boy name again? He played with Fesh.
Come on.
We were talking about Jack Carey. Zeb. Zeb. He was on Clarinet. On Clarinet.
The instructor Clarinet.
Yeah, yeah. Zeb. And I can't think of his... Who was the coronet? What's that fellow's name? Didn't he have a brother? Oh, Mutt.
Mutt, yeah, Mutt.

I just wondered if you know Punch played with him too a while. Yeah, I don't remember, but I know Punch from racing, you know. Punch is a player in racing. That's why he met me with Gabriel, see? Well you knew Punch out there in the country. Oh yeah, oh yeah. Yeah, sure.
I guess he was born, I remember.

Yeah, he was born already. He come up around all together, you know. Did he play with you out there then? No, he never played with us. That's why I say we was a regular band, you see. Yes. We just stuck together every time you see the band, well you see the same face, you see. That's why I never had a chance to play with no band, being with Gabriel, because then Gabriel later on he quit us, you know. Then that made us four brothers had our own band, you see.
Had your own band, yes. Yeah, our own band, you see. What did you call that? The James Brothers. James Brothers. Uh huh.
Yeah.
About the same size band, would that be?
Yeah, about the same size band. Fifteen pieces? No, no, that's a brass band. No, that's a string band.
Oh, how many pieces did you have?
Well, the Gabriel band band, how many? You had six pieces in the Gabriel band.
He had slide and trombone, he had his violin, guitar, bass, drums and trumpets. Oh, I see, yeah.
Uh huh. And then your own band, when you had the James Brothers band. We had the same amount.
Same.
Same instruments.

Yeah, well, let me see, I had saxophone and clarinet, bass, and drums and trumpet. Oh, yeah. Yeah. Who was the trumpet with your band? Uh, Ollie Drefflin. He was out of Thibodeau, right? Yeah, yeah, from Shrebus, Louisiana. Ollie Drefflin. Then we had at one time, Bunk used to come out there and play with us. Oh, Bunk played with us? Yeah, yeah. And, uh, just all of them.
Where was Bunk living in those days? Do you remember where Bunk was living?

Bunk was living now and yet. Here in New Orleans went out? Yeah, yeah, he went out there. Because Bunk lived out of New Iberia, you know, a long time too. Yeah, yeah, well, he played with Gabriel, uh, when he was in New Iberia, see. He come out and played. We'd spit up our band whenever we'd get him, see. I was with Gabriel then. I knew Bunk very well.
How did he play in those days? I never knew him in the old days.
Bunk was a little, you know, was a good trumpet player. That's right, yeah. Well, and his style, you see. That's why I say the style that he played in, well, it'll always be music. You see?
Yeah, I think so.

That's what gets you, see. When the fellow plays the style that you like his style, well, that's music. But now this rock and roll stuff, a fellow might pick out a couple of numbers and all and make it famous and get famous, but put him to continue that, well, he can't make it, you see. That's why I say I wouldn't want to catch myself playing with musicians just that way. I want to get with the best, see. And that would make me move there, see. Yeah, quite right. But now I can get to those fellows and people think I can't play. It's just like reading. Well, now, I can read, but I'm afraid to take a chance at it because I don't wear no glasses. My sight is bad, but you see all that. I wouldn't want to call myself, put myself in a reading van and knowing my weakness, you see. Well, I wouldn't want them to say that I can't do it, you see. But if I just have to do it, I'll always make some reservations to do it, you see. It's just like my clarinet now. Now I've got false teeth, see. I've been trying to blow with my teeth, but I'm going to have to take my top plate out whenever I get to want to play clarinet, see.
When you played the clarinet, even when you had your own teeth, did you bite onto the mouthpiece with your teeth,
or use your lips? No, no, I used my lips. Yeah.
Covered the upper teeth with your lips. Yeah, yeah. Did anybody teach you to do that, this fellow there? No, no. That's what I said.
I just picked it up and just, you know.
Professor Minetta says that Sam Dutre taught him to do that. Oh, yeah. Oh, he was, he was, he was. Do you remember George Barquet, did he, did he bit? Well, I don't remember. You don't remember.
